**English draft for R5 review.**

Some numbers are **secret**, like the key to your house. An **OTP** (a code that comes on the phone), a **PIN** and a **password** are secret keys.

Never tell them to anyone. Not to a caller, not to a friend, not even to someone who says they are from a bank.

If someone asks, say **"No"** and tell a grown-up you trust. A good password is long and not your name or birthday.

Gullak uses virtual play money only.

questions.prompt: Someone on the phone asks for the code that came on Mummy's phone. What do you do?

options.text: Say no and tell a grown-up

questions.explanation: Secret codes are never shared. Tell a trusted adult.

questions.prompt: A game asks for your home address. What should you do first?
questions.explanation: Always ask a grown-up before sharing personal details.
Long passwords that aren't about you are hardest to guess.

variants.markdown:
**English draft for R5 review.**

Most account takeovers in India don't break encryption; they trick people into handing over a **second factor**. An OTP is a one-time key for one action. A caller who asks for it is trying to complete a payment, login or SIM swap in your name. **No bank, wallet or government office ever asks for OTPs, PINs, CVVs or passwords.**

Your **identity data** also has value. A photo of an Aadhaar or PAN card can be misused to open loans or SIMs. When sharing ID, use a masked Aadhaar where possible and write the purpose on the copy ("for hostel admission only").

For passwords, length beats complexity: a **passphrase** of four unrelated words is stronger and easier to remember than a short mix of symbols. Use a **different password for every important account**, because one leaked site otherwise unlocks the rest. Turn on **two-factor authentication** and, ideally, use a password manager.

Watch the warning signs of **social engineering**: urgency, authority ("I'm from the bank/police"), secrecy and a request for a code.

Gullak uses virtual play money only.

questions.prompt: Why does a scammer want an OTP you just received?

options.text: To complete a payment or login in your name

questions.explanation: The OTP authorises an action; giving it hands that action to them.

questions.prompt: Why use a different password for each important account?

options.text: One leaked site shouldn't unlock the others

questions.explanation: Password reuse lets one breach spread to every account.

questions.prompt: You must share an ID copy for hostel admission. What reduces misuse?

options.text: Send the full Aadhaar on social media
Use a masked Aadhaar and write the purpose on the copy
Send it to anyone who asks

questions.explanation: Masking and purpose-marking limit what a stolen copy can do.

questions.prompt: Which mix is a classic social-engineering pattern?

options.text: Urgent, authoritative, secret and asking for a code

questions.explanation: Urgency, authority, secrecy and a code request together signal a scam.
